Title: Mobile application for digital extension and advisory services (IDEAS) to support smallholder chicken farmers in poultry production and management
Description: This is an interactive digital extension and advisory service app (IDEAS) to leverage various components of poultry production and provide inclusive support to smallholder poultry farmers. This App is primarily designed to support farmers in identification and access to chicken breeds available in each country, formulation and use of locally available feeds, disease prevention and treatment, market information, and linkages, creating a platform for discussion and knowledge sharing, and real-time advisory and support services. It is developed in various languages and comprises various visual, interactive, text, and video features that can deliver tailored services for smallholder poultry farmers.

Title: Multiplication and dissemination business model, for tropically-adapted and farmer-preferred improved chicken breeds, for value-chain actors, research and development partners in Lower and Middle Income Countries (LMIC)
Description: The scaling business model is proposed based on approaches as suggested by Lundy et al. (2012) that includes three major steps. First, mapping the existing business model using the nine caveats and identifying major challenges and opportunities. The existing business model was mapped using data from baseline and marketing assessment surveys focusing on inputs supply, production, marketing, institutional support, vertical and horizontal coordination along the value chain. Second, identifying business cases using lessons learned from previous tropical poultry genetics solution activities in Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Third, developing the new business model considering the business cases identified above. The proposed scaling business model has six  major components: establishing partnership, organizing and building capacity, access to inputs and services (i.e . feed, heath, finance, breed, training and extension services), production and support, value addition and marketing (through aggregators, wholesalers, retailers and processors), monitoring and optimization.

1. Introduction
Smallholder poultry production is integral to rural and agricultural households’ livelihood in developing countries, including Africa and Asia. Various studies show that smallholder poultry production significantly contributes to household income, food and nutritional security ( Wong et al. 2017; Birhanu et al. 2023b). It also has a sizable contribution to women’s empowerment and job creation. However, despite various research and development efforts in the previous decades, the production and productivity of the sector have remained quite low due to multiple production, marketing, policy and institutional constraints (Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al., 2023a; Anyona et al. 2023). Most farmers keep small flock sizes, mainly using low-input, low-output production practices for subsistence and income generation. Producers have limited access to better inputs and output markets, with weak horizontal and vertical coordination and linkages. Moreover, poultry product demand is highly seasonal, and there is significant price fluctuation associated with socioeconomic and cultural factors (Birhanu et al. 2022). Higher transaction costs, limited access to roads and other infrastructure, limited bargaining power and limited access to information restrict household access to better markets. Transforming the sector from subsistence-based to market-oriented commercial production requires integrated interventions, including improved genetics, health, feed, management practices, access to extension and advisory services, access to finance, capacity building, market linkages, collective actions and coordination ( Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al. 2022; Yakubu et al. 2023).
An increasing trend in poultry product consumption—associated with increasing population, urbanization, increasing income of the middle-class population, and preference for white meat over red meat—has created opportunities and challenges for smallholder producers. The opportunities could be associated with a broader market for eggs and meat. At the same time, the challenges would be strong competition with the emerging commercial sector in peri-urban and urban areas. An increasing demand in urban areas requires standardized products and better production and management practices from smallholders. However, given their large number and dispersed in remote locations, where there are significant infrastructural, institutional, technical, and policy-related challenges, individually, smallholder farmers cannot cope with existing and emerging challenges and exploit opportunities. Organizing farmers enhances collective actions, peer-to-peer learning, and access to inputs and output markets such as improved breeds, feeds, health services, finance, training, and advisory services (Fischer and Qaim 2014; Mutonyi 2019; Missiame et al. 2023). Moreover, sustained access to better inputs and value-added output markets requires strategies to link producers to different market opportunities.
Based on the above backgrounds, as part of the CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING), the Tropical Poultry Genetics Solution (TPGS) is implementing different interventions that enhance the production and productivity of the sector including developing a business model for scaling improved tropically adapted breeds. The scaling business model involves organizing farmers in groups and linking them with inputs, suppliers, and marketing actors for sustained adoption and use of farmer-preferred and locally adapted breeds. Considering the vital role of organizing farmers in groups and creating market linkage, this document is developed as a reference material when establishing farmer groups/organizations and linking them with various input suppliers, service providers, and marketing actors. The document is generic and can be applied to smallholder-based agricultural production and marketing activities. However, the proposed approaches can be amended and adjusted based on the country’s local contexts, policies, and strategies.
2. The role of group formation in smallholder agricultural production
Most smallholder farmers live in rural areas in highly dispersed locations and far from input and output markets. These areas have poor rural infrastructure, weak institutions, limited access to markets and services, limited information and low access to innovative technologies. They experience multiple production, marketing and consumption challenges that individual actions cannot easily address but require collective actions (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Ruzzante et al. 2021). Empirical evidence suggests that organizing farmers in groups is a good strategy for addressing most of the production and marketing challenges (Birhanu et al. 2017; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2018; Bachke 2019; Abdul- Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Bizikova et al. 2020; Bairagi and Mottaleb 2021; Ma et al. 2023; Tran et al. 2023).
Farmer organizations can be defined as groups formed to address the different interests of farmers. These organizations can be formal or informal and have different forms, including cooperatives, associations, self-help groups and commodity-based producer organizations (CRS and MEAS 2015; Bizikova et al. 2020; Fernando et al. 2021). Farmer organizations can also be classified into three board categories: general interest groups, cooperatives and commodity-based organizations. Interest groups represent farmers’ interests in policy and program development, mobilize resources and information for farmers, organize capacity building and address other issues that attract farmers’ interest. Cooperatives are business organizations owned and managed by farmers and other actors in the value chain to fulfill members’ needs for agricultural inputs and services and create demand for their produce. Usually, cooperatives facilitate the distribution of agricultural inputs, collect, store and add value to products, deliver large quantities to markets, and provide other services such as credit, savings and insurance. Commodity-based organizations are specialized groups of farmers organized based on a specific crop or livestock commodity that comprises various actors in the value chain, including producers, marketing actors, and input and service providers. Farmers’ organizations can function at different levels, such as village, kebele, district or region. Usually, the groups are independent, non-governmental and voluntary.
The essential role of organizing farmers in groups is documented in various empirical studies (Markelova and Mwangi 2010; Shiferaw et al. 2011; CRS and MEAS 2015; Agarwal, 2018; Gugerty et al. 2019; Bizikova et al. 2020; Kassie et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2023). Farmer groups enhance collective actions that reduce transaction costs and help to obtain better market prices (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020). Organized farmers can take advantage of economies of scale, express their needs, have better lobbying ability, and be in a good position for buying inputs and bulking and selling outputs. When farmers are organized, their voices can be easily heard, and their contribution to the research and development agenda can be significant. On the other hand, isolated and individual actions of farmers restrict them from fulfilling their production and marketing objectives due to limited access to input and output markets, inadequate capital, technical and social capacity, and other institutional and organizational factors. Organized farmers can easily access technology through linkages with service and input providers, including the research and extension system. Research and development institutes are also more likely to work with a group of farmers than individual farmers. Farmers who participated in farm organizations or groups have been found to have better economic and social gains compared with others (Shiferaw et al. 2011; Abebaw and Haile 2013; Abate et al. 2014; Verhofstadt and Maertens 2014; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020).
As indicated above, a sustained transformation of traditional smallholder-based poultry production requires organizing farmers in groups for collective actions and establishing effective linkages along the value chain. Organizing farmers helps to promote farmer adoption of improved production and marketing practices; enhance service delivery; reduce transaction costs; improve farmers’ bargaining power; encourage farm work; empower rural women; improve members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and improve
value additions. When smallholder poultry farmers are organized, they can easily access improved technologies such as poultry breeds, feeds, vaccines, treatment drugs, and other assets such as feeders and drinkers. Moreover, farmers organized in groups can be suitable partners for research and development activities.

2.1 Stage I: Startups
2.1.1 Step 1: Define the goal and scope of the proposed group formation
The formation of farmers’ groups should be based on clear and achievable objectives with predefined scopes, without unrealistic assumptions. Objectives of group formation may include enhancing access to technologies and better management practices, improving technical efficiency, access to better markets and credit; empowering women through different strategies; enhancing members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and increasing participation in the value chain through value addition (Francesconi and Wouterse 2015; Di Marcantonio et al. 2022). The groups should be manageable and organized by homogeneous people with similar interests and economic conditions.

2.1.2 Step 2: Understand the characteristics of target farmers
Smallholder farmers in developing countries are very heterogeneous. However, farmers in different geographies have specific characteristics and interests in production and marketing activities that differentiate them from others. Hence, understanding the target farmers’ characteristics is critical to establishing a successful farmer organization. This could be done through formal and informal approaches, including quick assessments regarding their interest in group work and vision for improved technologies-based production and marketing activities. Farmer characteristics may include age and gender composition, social and cultural settings that affect group formation, practices in farm and non-farm activities, average income, assets holding, land sizes, distance to main roads, and other socioeconomic activities associated with poultry production practices. At this stage, it is also important to know if the target farmers are part of existing farmers’ groups, have experience participating in similar groups and are interested in joining the proposed poultry-based groups.
2.1.3 Step 3: Identify potential leaders
The success and failure of farmers’ organizations depend partly on leadership style and management skills. Partners who facilitate the formation of the proposed farmer groups must ensure the presence of potential leaders among the target groups. Potential leaders can be identified using predefined criteria, including experience in group/community leadership, interest in leading the group, communication skills, education, technical skills and interest in poultry-based business. The potential leaders should include a mix of people from different age and gender groups.
2.1.4 Step 4: Talk to the local community leaders/administrators
Engaging local administrators and partners on the ground is vital to the sustainability of the proposed group formation. From the inception stage, local administrators should be involved through formal and informal meetings and discussion forums. The facilitating team can arrange a brief meeting and discuss the need to organize farmers, their alignment with the country’s policy, and their contribution to the development of the poultry sector. Facilitators should clarify the goal and scope of the proposed group formation, create awareness, and receive the necessary feedback and support from the community leaders and other stakeholders on the ground. Community leaders and farmer-organizing units should be part of the implementing partners.
2.1.5 Step 5: Establish the group
Once the goal and scope of the proposed group are defined, farmers are characterized, potential leaders are identified, and community leaders and partners are engaged, a community awareness meeting can be held to promote the idea and encourage targeted farmers to join the group. At this stage, interested farmers can be registered using appropriate formats. This meeting can clarify the needs and goals of group formation, nominate the identified leaders, obtain approvals and formally establish the groups. In this meeting, the need to develop a farmers’ group should be explained to participants, and farmers could ask questions to get clarification on important issues and share their expectations of participating in the group. The members can also elect potential member farmers who can work in different roles for the next few years.
2.1.6 Step 6: Develop the organizational structure
Facilitators and elected leaders can develop the organizational structure of the group. However, facilitators and group leaders may not start from scratch and can tailor and adopt similar organizational structures used in different farmer groups in their local or other areas. The organizational structure in the proposed farmer groups should reflect various relationships between the members of the groups, and facilitators and group leaders can choose from various options that maximize individual contributions while minimizing challenges (Bolman and Deal 2017). The organizational structure should show the types of committee members, the roles and responsibilities of different committee members, directions of information flow, and decision-making processes. As a starting point, the structure should be simple and easily amendable at any time and able to be developed with technical help from other local partners. 2.2.1 Step 7: Build the capacity of the group
Building the capacity of group leaders and other members is important for establishing successful groups (Ashby et al. 2009). As indicated above, leadership plays a critical role in the success and sustainability of group formation. Among other things, facilitating teams and partners on the ground should focus on raising good leaders through capacity building. The capacity-building efforts should focus on multiple dimensions of group formation, such as productive, organizational, entrepreneurial and sociopolitical dimensions (Valleur 2017). This can be achieved through formal and informal training, experience sharing, coaching and advisory services, and financial and material support. Various trainings can be provided on identified issues that help fulfill the groups’ missions and goals. Nevertheless, capacity- building efforts should be planned and properly implemented with partners and stakeholders. For instance, capacity building in time management, such as long meetings, record keeping, leadership style, fairness and communication, will significantly contribute to the success of group formation (CRS and MEAS 2015). The role of capacity building at the initial stage of group formation is documented in some empirical studies (Ahado et al. 2021).
2.2.2 Step 8: Plan and implement activities
After establishing the farmers’ group and capacity building, based on the goals of the group formation, potential interventions that improve the production and marketing activities of the group members should be identified, planned and implemented. This may involve identifying and analyzing problems, identifying possible solutions, prioritizing issues and
solutions, checking the feasibility of solutions, and developing detailed action plans (CRS and MEAS 2015). Activities should be prioritized and ranked based on importance and available resources, considering the farmers’ existing situation and local conditions. For smallholder poultry producers, this may include linking the groups with input suppliers, service providers and marketing actors; identifying and promoting additional value chain activities such as establishing product aggregation and marketing centres; adding more people to the group; expanding production and marketing activities; and building the technical skills of farmers. The group leaders should adopt dynamic approaches in implementing the proposed activities.
2.3 Stage III: Regular activities
2.3.1 Step 9: Monitoring and evaluation
Monitoring and evaluation should be integral to the group formation process and the entire management system. The monitoring component refers to keeping regular records of group activities, verifying that planned actions are taken according to the plan and adjusting ongoing activities to align with the group’s goals. On the other hand, evaluation may refer to looking back to confirm whether the proposed objectives have been met and identifying strategies to improve future activities to meet the group’s mission (CRS and MEAS 2015). Monitoring and evaluation activities can follow a participatory approach and are conducted jointly by group leaders, facilitators, local partners and other stakeholders. This would be led by the facilitating institution supported by other stockholders supporting this activity. One of the main responsibilities of facilitators would be establishing the monitoring evaluation system as part of supporting the proposed group and documenting lessons learned for scaling in different areas.
3. Linking organized groups with inputs and output markets
3.1. Market linkages and smallholder farmers
In most developing countries, the smallholder poultry value chain is characterized by low production and productivity with limited competitive advantage with emerging commercial sectors in urban and peri-urban areas. Access to inputs and output markets is the main constraint identified by almost all empirical studies on technology adoption and productivity (Adesina et al. 2014). Findings from such studies suggest linking smallholder farmers with input suppliers and central markets as essential interventions to enhance production and productivity and transform the sector from subsistence-based production to commercial production (Ebata and Hernandez 2017; Birhanu et al. 2022). Farmers’ participation in market-oriented production enhances household income, nutrition, job opportunities and other livelihood activities. Therefore, linking farmers with value chain actors using various strategies is one of the best approaches to enhance smallholders’ access to input and output markets. Linking farmers with inputs and output markets is not establishing an ad-hoc sale but developing long-term and formal business relationships among various value chain actors (Shepherd 2007). However, as indicated above, farmers must first be organized to establish effective linkages, as organized groups can be easily linked with various value chain actors.
Farmers’ linkage arrangements may consist of service provision (such as the delivery of improved breeds, vaccines, drugs, feeds, other assets such as feeders and drinkers, and providing training and advisory services); investing in value chain activities; formal and
informal contractual agreements; purchasing arrangements for outputs; full vertical cooperation with other value chain actors; asset sharing; contract farming; and other informal linkages and ad hoc arrangements (Dannson et al. 2004; Ferris et al. 2014b). For sustained adoption of technologies and improved livelihood outcomes, farmers can be primarily linked with input suppliers, such as improved breeds, feed and vaccine and treatment drug suppliers, and output markets with traders and institutional buyers, such as school feeding programs, universities and hospitals. To begin with, facilitators may focus on linking organized farmer groups with local input suppliers using various approaches. This process should involve local partners and stakeholders in government offices and non- government organizations working on input and output market linkages.
Strategies for creating market linkages can be broadly categorized into input and output market linkages (Figure 2). Although both adopt similar approaches, examining them separately helps to understand some of the specific issues among input and output marketing actors. Inputs market linkages involve exploring farmers’ needs and requirements; identifying potential inputs and service suppliers and initiating linkages; enhancing farmers’ awareness and understanding; organizing a joint discussion forum and determining the linkage type; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation. Linking with output markets involves establishing product collection/aggregation centers; identifying potential buyers/markets; organizing a discussion forum between producers and buyers; specifying contracts and developing risk management strategies; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation.

3.2 Strategies for creating linkages with input suppliers
Establishing successful and long-term inputs market linkage requires well-thought-out and carefully planned activities based on the context of each location. The linkage created should be based on win-win principles, where smallholder producers, input and service providers, and marketing actors benefit mutually. Establishing sustained inputs market linkages involves the following activities.
3.2.1 Explore farmers’ needs and requirements
Working with individual farmers involves higher transaction costs for companies or firms, and organizing them in groups should be an important step, as indicated above. To establish successful linkage, it is important to understand farmers’ production objectives, gender and age compositions, production and marketing practices, available resources for scaling existing production activity, production environment, and their current and potential capacity for market-originated production.
The smallholder farmers’ demand for inputs and the service requirement usually depend on their production objectives, the adopted technologies, the technical and financial capacity, and other socioeconomic factors. The production practice they adopt (intensive vs extensive production) also determines their input type. Moreover, farmers in each area may not always need all the recommended commercial inputs, as they can also use locally available sources or a mix of locally available and commercial inputs.
Despite the dynamic nature, it is essential to understand the type, quality and volume of inputs and services required by farmers in each period. Although this needs continuous assessment, it can generally be achieved using a mix of approaches, including formal assessments such as checklists of inputs and services required by farmers and their willingness and ability to pay for the inputs.
3.2.2 Identify potential inputs and service providers and initiate linkages
Due to asymmetric information and inadequate capacity and skills, smallholder farmers have limited ability to identify appropriate input suppliers and service providers. Since most of them live in rural areas with minimal access to roads, information and other infrastructures, they have limited capacity to access most value chain actors. Therefore, facilitators must first identify potential input suppliers (i.e., individuals, companies, etc.) relevant to smallholder farmers and begin a discussion with them to initiate the linkages. This may primarily involve identifying the inputs farmers require for production and marketing activities and the capacity and willingness of suppliers to work with smallholder farmers in each target location. This could be done through a rapid assessment, including reviewing the company’s expertise and activities, collecting customer information, key informant interviews, and reviewing documents. Working with existing commercial companies would be the best strategy for the poultry sector. Facilitators can approach commercial poultry companies or agents that can supply key inputs such as improved breeds in the area and major feed, vaccine and drug suppliers.

1. Introduction
Smallholder poultry production is integral to rural and agricultural households’ livelihood in developing countries, including Africa and Asia. Various studies show that smallholder poultry production significantly contributes to household income, food and nutritional security ( Wong et al. 2017; Birhanu et al. 2023b). It also has a sizable contribution to women’s empowerment and job creation. However, despite various research and development efforts in the previous decades, the production and productivity of the sector have remained quite low due to multiple production, marketing, policy and institutional constraints (Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al., 2023a; Anyona et al. 2023). Most farmers keep small flock sizes, mainly using low-input, low-output production practices for subsistence and income generation. Producers have limited access to better inputs and output markets, with weak horizontal and vertical coordination and linkages. Moreover, poultry product demand is highly seasonal, and there is significant price fluctuation associated with socioeconomic and cultural factors (Birhanu et al. 2022). Higher transaction costs, limited access to roads and other infrastructure, limited bargaining power and limited access to information restrict household access to better markets. Transforming the sector from subsistence-based to market-oriented commercial production requires integrated interventions, including improved genetics, health, feed, management practices, access to extension and advisory services, access to finance, capacity building, market linkages, collective actions and coordination ( Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al. 2022; Yakubu et al. 2023).
An increasing trend in poultry product consumption—associated with increasing population, urbanization, increasing income of the middle-class population, and preference for white meat over red meat—has created opportunities and challenges for smallholder producers. The opportunities could be associated with a broader market for eggs and meat. At the same time, the challenges would be strong competition with the emerging commercial sector in peri-urban and urban areas. An increasing demand in urban areas requires standardized products and better production and management practices from smallholders. However, given their large number and dispersed in remote locations, where there are significant infrastructural, institutional, technical, and policy-related challenges, individually, smallholder farmers cannot cope with existing and emerging challenges and exploit opportunities. Organizing farmers enhances collective actions, peer-to-peer learning, and access to inputs and output markets such as improved breeds, feeds, health services, finance, training, and advisory services (Fischer and Qaim 2014; Mutonyi 2019; Missiame et al. 2023). Moreover, sustained access to better inputs and value-added output markets requires strategies to link producers to different market opportunities.
Based on the above backgrounds, as part of the CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING), the Tropical Poultry Genetics Solution (TPGS) is implementing different interventions that enhance the production and productivity of the sector including developing a business model for scaling improved tropically adapted breeds. The scaling business model involves organizing farmers in groups and linking them with inputs, suppliers, and marketing actors for sustained adoption and use of farmer-preferred and locally adapted breeds. Considering the vital role of organizing farmers in groups and creating market linkage, this document is developed as a reference material when establishing farmer groups/organizations and linking them with various input suppliers, service providers, and marketing actors. The document is generic and can be applied to smallholder-based agricultural production and marketing activities. However, the proposed approaches can be amended and adjusted based on the country’s local contexts, policies, and strategies.
2. The role of group formation in smallholder agricultural production
Most smallholder farmers live in rural areas in highly dispersed locations and far from input and output markets. These areas have poor rural infrastructure, weak institutions, limited access to markets and services, limited information and low access to innovative technologies. They experience multiple production, marketing and consumption challenges that individual actions cannot easily address but require collective actions (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Ruzzante et al. 2021). Empirical evidence suggests that organizing farmers in groups is a good strategy for addressing most of the production and marketing challenges (Birhanu et al. 2017; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2018; Bachke 2019; Abdul- Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Bizikova et al. 2020; Bairagi and Mottaleb 2021; Ma et al. 2023; Tran et al. 2023).
Farmer organizations can be defined as groups formed to address the different interests of farmers. These organizations can be formal or informal and have different forms, including cooperatives, associations, self-help groups and commodity-based producer organizations (CRS and MEAS 2015; Bizikova et al. 2020; Fernando et al. 2021). Farmer organizations can also be classified into three board categories: general interest groups, cooperatives and commodity-based organizations. Interest groups represent farmers’ interests in policy and program development, mobilize resources and information for farmers, organize capacity building and address other issues that attract farmers’ interest. Cooperatives are business organizations owned and managed by farmers and other actors in the value chain to fulfill members’ needs for agricultural inputs and services and create demand for their produce. Usually, cooperatives facilitate the distribution of agricultural inputs, collect, store and add value to products, deliver large quantities to markets, and provide other services such as credit, savings and insurance. Commodity-based organizations are specialized groups of farmers organized based on a specific crop or livestock commodity that comprises various actors in the value chain, including producers, marketing actors, and input and service providers. Farmers’ organizations can function at different levels, such as village, kebele, district or region. Usually, the groups are independent, non-governmental and voluntary.
The essential role of organizing farmers in groups is documented in various empirical studies (Markelova and Mwangi 2010; Shiferaw et al. 2011; CRS and MEAS 2015; Agarwal, 2018; Gugerty et al. 2019; Bizikova et al. 2020; Kassie et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2023). Farmer groups enhance collective actions that reduce transaction costs and help to obtain better market prices (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020). Organized farmers can take advantage of economies of scale, express their needs, have better lobbying ability, and be in a good position for buying inputs and bulking and selling outputs. When farmers are organized, their voices can be easily heard, and their contribution to the research and development agenda can be significant. On the other hand, isolated and individual actions of farmers restrict them from fulfilling their production and marketing objectives due to limited access to input and output markets, inadequate capital, technical and social capacity, and other institutional and organizational factors. Organized farmers can easily access technology through linkages with service and input providers, including the research and extension system. Research and development institutes are also more likely to work with a group of farmers than individual farmers. Farmers who participated in farm organizations or groups have been found to have better economic and social gains compared with others (Shiferaw et al. 2011; Abebaw and Haile 2013; Abate et al. 2014; Verhofstadt and Maertens 2014; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020).
As indicated above, a sustained transformation of traditional smallholder-based poultry production requires organizing farmers in groups for collective actions and establishing effective linkages along the value chain. Organizing farmers helps to promote farmer adoption of improved production and marketing practices; enhance service delivery; reduce transaction costs; improve farmers’ bargaining power; encourage farm work; empower rural women; improve members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and improve
value additions. When smallholder poultry farmers are organized, they can easily access improved technologies such as poultry breeds, feeds, vaccines, treatment drugs, and other assets such as feeders and drinkers. Moreover, farmers organized in groups can be suitable partners for research and development activities.
2.1 Approaches for organizing farmers
Although there is no single best approach to organize framers in groups, based on various empirical evidence suggested by researchers and development experts working in the area (CRS and MEAS 2015; Kassie et al. 2020), the following approaches can be adopted for smallholder poultry producers in developing countries. The approaches can be broadly classified into three stages and nine steps (Figure 1). The institutions that facilitate1 the group formation or organizing of farmers should have a good understanding of the sector and part Startup of the value chain actors.

2.1 Stage I: Startups
2.1.1 Step 1: Define the goal and scope of the proposed group formation
The formation of farmers’ groups should be based on clear and achievable objectives with predefined scopes, without unrealistic assumptions. Objectives of group formation may include enhancing access to technologies and better management practices, improving technical efficiency, access to better markets and credit; empowering women through different strategies; enhancing members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and increasing participation in the value chain through value addition (Francesconi and Wouterse 2015; Di Marcantonio et al. 2022). The groups should be manageable and organized by homogeneous people with similar interests and economic conditions.

2.1.2 Step 2: Understand the characteristics of target farmers
Smallholder farmers in developing countries are very heterogeneous. However, farmers in different geographies have specific characteristics and interests in production and marketing activities that differentiate them from others. Hence, understanding the target farmers’ characteristics is critical to establishing a successful farmer organization. This could be done through formal and informal approaches, including quick assessments regarding their interest in group work and vision for improved technologies-based production and marketing activities. Farmer characteristics may include age and gender composition, social and cultural settings that affect group formation, practices in farm and non-farm activities, average income, assets holding, land sizes, distance to main roads, and other socioeconomic activities associated with poultry production practices. At this stage, it is also important to know if the target farmers are part of existing farmers’ groups, have experience participating in similar groups and are interested in joining the proposed poultry-based groups.
2.1.3 Step 3: Identify potential leaders
The success and failure of farmers’ organizations depend partly on leadership style and management skills. Partners who facilitate the formation of the proposed farmer groups must ensure the presence of potential leaders among the target groups. Potential leaders can be identified using predefined criteria, including experience in group/community leadership, interest in leading the group, communication skills, education, technical skills and interest in poultry-based business. The potential leaders should include a mix of people from different age and gender groups.
2.1.4 Step 4: Talk to the local community leaders/administrators
Engaging local administrators and partners on the ground is vital to the sustainability of the proposed group formation. From the inception stage, local administrators should be involved through formal and informal meetings and discussion forums. The facilitating team can arrange a brief meeting and discuss the need to organize farmers, their alignment with the country’s policy, and their contribution to the development of the poultry sector. Facilitators should clarify the goal and scope of the proposed group formation, create awareness, and receive the necessary feedback and support from the community leaders and other stakeholders on the ground. Community leaders and farmer-organizing units should be part of the implementing partners.
2.1.5 Step 5: Establish the group
Once the goal and scope of the proposed group are defined, farmers are characterized, potential leaders are identified, and community leaders and partners are engaged, a community awareness meeting can be held to promote the idea and encourage targeted farmers to join the group. At this stage, interested farmers can be registered using appropriate formats. This meeting can clarify the needs and goals of group formation, nominate the identified leaders, obtain approvals and formally establish the groups. In this meeting, the need to develop a farmers’ group should be explained to participants, and farmers could ask questions to get clarification on important issues and share their expectations of participating in the group. The members can also elect potential member farmers who can work in different roles for the next few years.
2.1.6 Step 6: Develop the organizational structure
Facilitators and elected leaders can develop the organizational structure of the group. However, facilitators and group leaders may not start from scratch and can tailor and adopt similar organizational structures used in different farmer groups in their local or other areas. The organizational structure in the proposed farmer groups should reflect various relationships between the members of the groups, and facilitators and group leaders can choose from various options that maximize individual contributions while minimizing challenges (Bolman and Deal 2017). The organizational structure should show the types of committee members, the roles and responsibilities of different committee members, directions of information flow, and decision-making processes. As a starting point, the structure should be simple and easily amendable at any time and able to be developed with technical help from other local partners. However, according to Bolman and Deal (2017), the following questions can be considered while organizing the group’s structure (Box 1).

2.2.1 Step 7: Build the capacity of the group
Building the capacity of group leaders and other members is important for establishing successful groups (Ashby et al. 2009). As indicated above, leadership plays a critical role in the success and sustainability of group formation. Among other things, facilitating teams and partners on the ground should focus on raising good leaders through capacity building. The capacity-building efforts should focus on multiple dimensions of group formation, such as productive, organizational, entrepreneurial and sociopolitical dimensions (Valleur 2017). This can be achieved through formal and informal training, experience sharing, coaching and advisory services, and financial and material support. Various trainings can be provided on identified issues that help fulfill the groups’ missions and goals. Nevertheless, capacity- building efforts should be planned and properly implemented with partners and stakeholders. For instance, capacity building in time management, such as long meetings, record keeping, leadership style, fairness and communication, will significantly contribute to the success of group formation (CRS and MEAS 2015). The role of capacity building at the initial stage of group formation is documented in some empirical studies (Ahado et al. 2021).
2.2.2 Step 8: Plan and implement activities
After establishing the farmers’ group and capacity building, based on the goals of the group formation, potential interventions that improve the production and marketing activities of the group members should be identified, planned and implemented. This may involve identifying and analyzing problems, identifying possible solutions, prioritizing issues and
solutions, checking the feasibility of solutions, and developing detailed action plans (CRS and MEAS 2015). Activities should be prioritized and ranked based on importance and available resources, considering the farmers’ existing situation and local conditions. For smallholder poultry producers, this may include linking the groups with input suppliers, service providers and marketing actors; identifying and promoting additional value chain activities such as establishing product aggregation and marketing centres; adding more people to the group; expanding production and marketing activities; and building the technical skills of farmers. The group leaders should adopt dynamic approaches in implementing the proposed activities.
2.3 Stage III: Regular activities
2.3.1 Step 9: Monitoring and evaluation
Monitoring and evaluation should be integral to the group formation process and the entire management system. The monitoring component refers to keeping regular records of group activities, verifying that planned actions are taken according to the plan and adjusting ongoing activities to align with the group’s goals. On the other hand, evaluation may refer to looking back to confirm whether the proposed objectives have been met and identifying strategies to improve future activities to meet the group’s mission (CRS and MEAS 2015). Monitoring and evaluation activities can follow a participatory approach and are conducted jointly by group leaders, facilitators, local partners and other stakeholders. This would be led by the facilitating institution supported by other stockholders supporting this activity. One of the main responsibilities of facilitators would be establishing the monitoring evaluation system as part of supporting the proposed group and documenting lessons learned for scaling in different areas.
3. Linking organized groups with inputs and output markets
3.1. Market linkages and smallholder farmers
In most developing countries, the smallholder poultry value chain is characterized by low production and productivity with limited competitive advantage with emerging commercial sectors in urban and peri-urban areas. Access to inputs and output markets is the main constraint identified by almost all empirical studies on technology adoption and productivity (Adesina et al. 2014). Findings from such studies suggest linking smallholder farmers with input suppliers and central markets as essential interventions to enhance production and productivity and transform the sector from subsistence-based production to commercial production (Ebata and Hernandez 2017; Birhanu et al. 2022). Farmers’ participation in market-oriented production enhances household income, nutrition, job opportunities and other livelihood activities. Therefore, linking farmers with value chain actors using various strategies is one of the best approaches to enhance smallholders’ access to input and output markets. Linking farmers with inputs and output markets is not establishing an ad-hoc sale but developing long-term and formal business relationships among various value chain actors (Shepherd 2007). However, as indicated above, farmers must first be organized to establish effective linkages, as organized groups can be easily linked with various value chain actors.
Farmers’ linkage arrangements may consist of service provision (such as the delivery of improved breeds, vaccines, drugs, feeds, other assets such as feeders and drinkers, and providing training and advisory services); investing in value chain activities; formal and
informal contractual agreements; purchasing arrangements for outputs; full vertical cooperation with other value chain actors; asset sharing; contract farming; and other informal linkages and ad hoc arrangements (Dannson et al. 2004; Ferris et al. 2014b). For sustained adoption of technologies and improved livelihood outcomes, farmers can be primarily linked with input suppliers, such as improved breeds, feed and vaccine and treatment drug suppliers, and output markets with traders and institutional buyers, such as school feeding programs, universities and hospitals. To begin with, facilitators may focus on linking organized farmer groups with local input suppliers using various approaches. This process should involve local partners and stakeholders in government offices and non- government organizations working on input and output market linkages.
Strategies for creating market linkages can be broadly categorized into input and output market linkages (Figure 2). Although both adopt similar approaches, examining them separately helps to understand some of the specific issues among input and output marketing actors. Inputs market linkages involve exploring farmers’ needs and requirements; identifying potential inputs and service suppliers and initiating linkages; enhancing farmers’ awareness and understanding; organizing a joint discussion forum and determining the linkage type; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation. Linking with output markets involves establishing product collection/aggregation centers; identifying potential buyers/markets; organizing a discussion forum between producers and buyers; specifying contracts and developing risk management strategies; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation.

3.2 Strategies for creating linkages with input suppliers
Establishing successful and long-term inputs market linkage requires well-thought-out and carefully planned activities based on the context of each location. The linkage created should be based on win-win principles, where smallholder producers, input and service providers, and marketing actors benefit mutually. Establishing sustained inputs market linkages involves the following activities.
3.2.1 Explore farmers’ needs and requirements
Working with individual farmers involves higher transaction costs for companies or firms, and organizing them in groups should be an important step, as indicated above. To establish successful linkage, it is important to understand farmers’ production objectives, gender and age compositions, production and marketing practices, available resources for scaling existing production activity, production environment, and their current and potential capacity for market-originated production.
The smallholder farmers’ demand for inputs and the service requirement usually depend on their production objectives, the adopted technologies, the technical and financial capacity, and other socioeconomic factors. The production practice they adopt (intensive vs extensive production) also determines their input type. Moreover, farmers in each area may not always need all the recommended commercial inputs, as they can also use locally available sources or a mix of locally available and commercial inputs.
Despite the dynamic nature, it is essential to understand the type, quality and volume of inputs and services required by farmers in each period. Although this needs continuous assessment, it can generally be achieved using a mix of approaches, including formal assessments such as checklists of inputs and services required by farmers and their willingness and ability to pay for the inputs.
3.2.2 Identify potential inputs and service providers and initiate linkages
Due to asymmetric information and inadequate capacity and skills, smallholder farmers have limited ability to identify appropriate input suppliers and service providers. Since most of them live in rural areas with minimal access to roads, information and other infrastructures, they have limited capacity to access most value chain actors. Therefore, facilitators must first identify potential input suppliers (i.e., individuals, companies, etc.) relevant to smallholder farmers and begin a discussion with them to initiate the linkages. This may primarily involve identifying the inputs farmers require for production and marketing activities and the capacity and willingness of suppliers to work with smallholder farmers in each target location. This could be done through a rapid assessment, including reviewing the company’s expertise and activities, collecting customer information, key informant interviews, and reviewing documents. Working with existing commercial companies would be the best strategy for the poultry sector. Facilitators can approach commercial poultry companies or agents that can supply key inputs such as improved breeds in the area and major feed, vaccine and drug suppliers.

Using the information generated from Steps 1 and 2, facilitators can quickly match farmers’ demand for products and services and the capacity and readiness of companies/individuals to supply the smallholder farmers. Title: Integrated nutrition education package to smallholder chicken keepers for increased consumption of animal source food (ASF) and improved nutritional status in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania
Description: The integrated nutrition education package is a nutrition-sensitive intervention that aims to enhance the consumption of chicken meat, eggs and other nutrient-dense foods and improve the nutritional status of smallholder farmers, most notably under-five children, lactating mothers and pregnant women. This activity will be embedded in the existing on-farm chicken performance testing program and it will be provided to smallholder farmers using digital and paper-based nutrition education tools. About SAPLING
CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed, and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes, contributing to women’s empowerment, and reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.

Background to training
The Tropical Poultry Genetics Solutions (TPGS) program, led by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), aims to enhance the consumption of chicken products through its nutrition-sensitive interventions in various countries, including Ethiopia and Kenya. The intervention focuses on promoting the consumption of chicken meat and eggs, primarily leveraging participating households in on-farm chicken testing as a foundational entry point. This intervention specifically targets children under five years of age, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and women of reproductive age. Women are disproportionately affected by nutritional deficiencies due to factors such as reproductive biology, low social status, poverty, and lack of education. Undernutrition diminishes women’s resilience and makes them more vulnerable during childbirth, increasing their susceptibility to infections and reducing their reserves for recovery from illnesses. Over the past 10 months, integrated nutrition education has been delivered to these target groups through digital and paper-based tools, featuring monthly interactive sessions, including demonstrations and cooking activities. Nutrition education has been provided to both TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and other non-participant farmers within the project villages in the two countries. This activity is linked to the CGIAR Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) Work Package 2— Innovations and practices for safe livestock-derived foods consumption as part of diverse diets.
Location and modality
The training was provided face-to-face and held in Kenya and Ethiopia.
Dates
This training was held from March–October 2024.
Who conducted the training?
The National Agricultural Research System of Ethiopia and Kenya, most notably the Central Ethiopia Agricultural Research Institute (CEARI) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) provided this training.
Objectives of the training
The main objectives of the training were:
Addressing Malnutrition
• To identify and address major malnutrition challenges faced by target communities, particularly among vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and children under two years.
Promote Animal Source Foods Consumption
• To promote the importance of consuming animal-source foods, especially chicken products (meat and eggs), rich in essential nutrients vital for growth, development, and overall health. This may include encouraging families to incorporate chicken and eggs into their daily diets to enhance dietary diversity and nutritional intake.
Enhancing Nutritional Awareness
• To assess and enhance current knowledge regarding the benefits of animal-source foods among community members. Identify knowledge gaps and inform the development of effective educational programs aimed at changing dietary behaviours. The initiative also seeks to foster
2
healthier eating habits by emphasizing the value of including chicken and eggs in meals, encouraging families to make informed dietary choices.
Community Engagement
• To encourage both participant and non-participant households to improve chicken production and consumption practices, ensuring that the intervention scaled out a diverse segment of the community. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of community engagement strategies to promote inclusivity. Furthermore, the initiative aims to establish a feedback mechanism to gather insights from participants about their dietary practices and attitudes toward animal-source foods, allowing for continuous improvement of educational programs.
Promote the utilization of technology
To leverage digital tools, such as a nutrition literacy application, to enhance learning about the benefits of animal-source foods and assess their uptake among farmers. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of technology in promoting better nutrition and reaching a wider audience to facilitate ongoing education regarding the importance of chicken products.
Training agenda
The training agenda includes a comprehensive overview of essential nutritional topics, focusing on five key sessions: “Why Nutrition Matters,” “Family Nutrition,” “Maternal Nutrition,” “Child Nutrition,” and “Hygiene and Sanitation.” Each session included thematic areas that emphasized the importance of nutrition at various life stages. Participants explored the significance of food groups, dietary diversification, and the crucial roles of chicken, eggs, and meat in promoting health and growth. Emphasis was placed on maternal nutritional needs during pregnancy and lactation, as well as optimal feeding practices for children from birth to 24 months. Additionally, the agenda highlighted safe food handling practices and the importance of hygiene in ensuring proper nutrition, ultimately aiming to enhance overall health and well-being within families.
Training participants
A total of 301 households participated in the nutrition education, with 230 from TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and 70 from non-participant households. In Ethiopia, 44 participants—36 from on-farm chicken performance testing participants and 8 from non-participant households—indicated interest from non-participant households. Comments or next steps
Following the completion of these training sessions, participants are expected to experience a positive behavioral change in their dietary consumption, leading to improved nutritional status. To support the ongoing impact of the training, we will graduate a select group of farmers as champions who will serve
3
as leaders in their communities, promoting sustainable practices and encouraging others to adopt healthier nutritional habits. These champions will play a vital role in ensuring the sustainability of project activities fostering a culture of improved nutrition within their households and among fellow farmers. Additionally, end-line data will be collected to assess the impact on nutritional status and consumption patterns, providing valuable insights into the effectiveness of the training and guiding future initiatives. This comprehensive approach aims to enhance individual health outcomes and build a resilient community committed to ongoing nutritional education and support.

This theme covers nutrition requirements for infants from birth to five years. It discusses the right food to give to infants after six months, quantities, frequency of feeding and consistency of the food. The aim is to promote dietary diversity in infants and ensure that proper child care and feeding practises are adheredto by the caretakers.

KEY MESSAGES
Put your baby to the breast within the first 30 minutes of birth. Initiating breastfeeding facilitates milk production and helps your uterus to go back to shape faster and controls bleeding after delivery.
Feed your baby breast milk only, not even water, during the first six months after birth. Each feed-ing session should take between 20 and 45 minutes.
Exclusive breastfeeding promotes the child’s adequate growth and development. It is always clean; contains antibodies that protect against diseases. Breastmilk is always ready and at the right temperature and is easy to digest. It contains enough water for the baby’s needs.
Breastfeed as often as your child wants especially at night. Your child might be hungry if he/she is fussing, sucking fingers, or moving lips.

• When the child is sick continue to breastfeed often, to help quick recovery and regain the weight lost. Even if your baby has diarrhea it is important to keep breastfeeding.

About SAPLING
CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed, and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes, contributing to women’s empowerment, and reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.
Acknowledgements
This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity. CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
1
Background to training
The Tropical Poultry Genetics Solutions (TPGS) program, led by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), aims to enhance the consumption of chicken products through its nutrition-sensitive interventions in various countries, including Ethiopia and Kenya. The intervention focuses on promoting the consumption of chicken meat and eggs, primarily leveraging participating households in on-farm chicken testing as a foundational entry point. This intervention specifically targets children under five years of age, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and women of reproductive age. Women are disproportionately affected by nutritional deficiencies due to factors such as reproductive biology, low social status, poverty, and lack of education. Undernutrition diminishes women’s resilience and makes them more vulnerable during childbirth, increasing their susceptibility to infections and reducing their reserves for recovery from illnesses. Over the past 10 months, integrated nutrition education has been delivered to these target groups through digital and paper-based tools, featuring monthly interactive sessions, including demonstrations and cooking activities. Nutrition education has been provided to both TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and other non-participant farmers within the project villages in the two countries. This activity is linked to the CGIAR Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) Work Package 2— Innovations and practices for safe livestock-derived foods consumption as part of diverse diets.
Location and modality
The training was provided face-to-face and held in Kenya and Ethiopia.
Dates
This training was held from March–October 2024.
Who conducted the training?
The National Agricultural Research System of Ethiopia and Kenya, most notably the Central Ethiopia Agricultural Research Institute (CEARI) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) provided this training.
Objectives of the training
The main objectives of the training were:
Addressing Malnutrition
• To identify and address major malnutrition challenges faced by target communities, particularly among vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and children under two years.
Promote Animal Source Foods Consumption
• To promote the importance of consuming animal-source foods, especially chicken products (meat and eggs), rich in essential nutrients vital for growth, development, and overall health. This may include encouraging families to incorporate chicken and eggs into their daily diets to enhance dietary diversity and nutritional intake.
Enhancing Nutritional Awareness
• To assess and enhance current knowledge regarding the benefits of animal-source foods among community members. Identify knowledge gaps and inform the development of effective educational programs aimed at changing dietary behaviours. The initiative also seeks to foster
2
healthier eating habits by emphasizing the value of including chicken and eggs in meals, encouraging families to make informed dietary choices.
Community Engagement
• To encourage both participant and non-participant households to improve chicken production and consumption practices, ensuring that the intervention scaled out a diverse segment of the community. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of community engagement strategies to promote inclusivity. Furthermore, the initiative aims to establish a feedback mechanism to gather insights from participants about their dietary practices and attitudes toward animal-source foods, allowing for continuous improvement of educational programs.
Promote the utilization of technology
To leverage digital tools, such as a nutrition literacy application, to enhance learning about the benefits of animal-source foods and assess their uptake among farmers. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of technology in promoting better nutrition and reaching a wider audience to facilitate ongoing education regarding the importance of chicken products.
Training agenda
The training agenda includes a comprehensive overview of essential nutritional topics, focusing on five key sessions: “Why Nutrition Matters,” “Family Nutrition,” “Maternal Nutrition,” “Child Nutrition,” and “Hygiene and Sanitation.” Each session included thematic areas that emphasized the importance of nutrition at various life stages. Participants explored the significance of food groups, dietary diversification, and the crucial roles of chicken, eggs, and meat in promoting health and growth. Emphasis was placed on maternal nutritional needs during pregnancy and lactation, as well as optimal feeding practices for children from birth to 24 months. Additionally, the agenda highlighted safe food handling practices and the importance of hygiene in ensuring proper nutrition, ultimately aiming to enhance overall health and well-being within families.
Training participants
A total of 301 households participated in the nutrition education, with 230 from TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and 70 from non-participant households. In Ethiopia, 44 participants—36 from on-farm chicken performance testing participants and 8 from non-participant households—indicated interest from non-participant households. In Kenya, however, 257 individuals, including 194 from TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participants and 63 from non-participant households, are shown in Table 1 below.

Comments or next steps
Following the completion of these training sessions, participants are expected to experience a positive behavioral change in their dietary consumption, leading to improved nutritional status. To support the ongoing impact of the training, we will graduate a select group of farmers as champions who will serve
3
as leaders in their communities, promoting sustainable practices and encouraging others to adopt healthier nutritional habits. These champions will play a vital role in ensuring the sustainability of project activities fostering a culture of improved nutrition within their households and among fellow farmers. Additionally, end-line data will be collected to assess the impact on nutritional status and consumption patterns, providing valuable insights into the effectiveness of the training and guiding future initiatives. This comprehensive approach aims to enhance individual health outcomes and build a resilient community committed to ongoing nutritional education and support.

Title: Optimized indigenous forages of Ethiopia for smallholder farmer small ruminant production
Description: In Ethiopia, livestock primarily consume indigenous forages, which are traditionally provided either fresh or after undergoing various processing methods. Farmers' preferences for using these forages is being assessed,  the nutritional value evaluated and the potential for further development and commercialization of different varieties of these forages explored.

Introduction
Agricultural research in Ethiopia began in the early 1960s. The earliest agricultural research center was the Debre Zeit Experiment Station, a constituent station of Alemaya College of Agriculture, Emperor Haile Selasie University. Almost at the same time, the national research system, IAR was established in 1966, by proclamation No 42/58 (1958 E.C.). The Swedish-Ethiopian regional agricultural development branch- the Arsi Rural Development Unit (ARDU) was founded in 1966 (SIDA, 1966), and became operational in 1972 (CADU, 1972). The CGIAR research institute, ILCA, was established in 1982 to promote livestock development in Africa. All these institutions did their part to improve livestock productivity through improving animal feed inter alia.
to improve livestock productivity through improving animal feed inter alia.
The scope of this review is limited to the topic of forage research in Ethiopia, with a focus on native Forage species. Therefore, the foregoing discussions do not go beyond simple presentation of stories of forage research processes, achievements, and gaps in the research, collected from published and unpublished literature found at various national and international research institutions.
From the research achievements of the pioneering institute CADU-ARDU, it is evident that wholistic, system-based research and development approaches were more fruitful than isolated single item-based approaches. Although sustenance could not be maintained for various reasons, there is evidence that improved forage crops developed by CADU have made their way to the farm gates of smallholder farmers in Arsi (ARDU, 1983). Additionally, CADU researchers have laid the groundwork for the fruitful approach of screening and developing varieties from indigenous material (Carlson, J., 1972; Thulin, M., 1972). Now, after half a century of research (with “staggering” achievements), benefits of focusing research efforts on native forages are vivid. Box 1.1 is a case in point.
A review of published and unpublished literature revealed that a total of 59 indigenous forage species (31 legumes and 28 grasses) have undergone evaluation for their forage value. Of these, 6 legume varieties and 9 grass varieties have been registered/released (NVRC, 2018). This number does not correspond to the exotic species that have been introduced and evaluated in the country since forage research began. Apart from a few species: Oats (Avena spp), Rhodes (Chloris gauana), Guinea grass (Panicum maximum), vetches (Vetch spp) Lucerne (Medicago sativa) desmodiums (Desmodium intortum and D. uncinatum) which remain valuable forage crops in districts of Ethiopia, other large numbers of introductions failed important selection criteria (adaptation, yield and quality). Some temperate grass species such as rye grass (Lolium spp) are destroyed by rust. Most of the previously selected and recommended oats varieties (Lulseged G. Hiwot, 1981), suffer from crown rust, although resistant varieties have been developed. Oats
1
remain the only successful annual forage grass species. The exotic clovers (Trifolium repens, T. pretense and others) cannot compete with the native clover species in terms of adaptability and herbage yield.
Box 1.1: Desho, the mysterious indigenous forage grass
Desho grass (Pennisetum glaucifolium) is an indigenous perennial grass forage variety developed from native ecotypes germplasm collected jointly by the Debre Zeit Agric Research Center (DZARC) and Areca Agricultural Research Center (AARC) of the Southern Nations Nationalities and Peoples Region (SNNPR) around Wolayta Zone. The grass is tussoky, rhizomatous, erect, up to 2 meters tall. The dense stem and foliage is glossy, so named glousifolius. Forage yield varies widely with soil fertility and moisture. Mean dry forage yield per harvest ranged 5.6 – 8.8 t/ha DM. While yearly (3 cuts) yield (under irrigation), ranged between 21.0 t/ha (Areka-DZF-590) to 24.59 t/ha (Kindukosha-DZF-591). At its best location (Wondo Genet) with fertile soil and abundant soil moisture, the mean DM yield ranged 25 – 39 t/ha (Solomon Mengistu et al, 2017; Tekalign Yirgu et al, 2017). Among the “pro-poor” forage technologies, three varieties of desho officially released by DZARC have provided hope to the smallholder farmer (Fig. 1). MoARD and NGOs have desiminated planting material almost throughout the highlands of Ethiopia. Farmers plant desho in their backyard on small plots and use the green fodder to feed lactating cows and young stock. Desho ha gained nationwide popularity. Some farmers have taken up multiplying propagation material as a business and make money by selling bunches of vegetative (stem cuttings and rhizome splits) to neigbouring farmers and even to distant areas, hundreds of kms away. The business has spread dramatically.

Various references in literature indicate that the screening and selection of forage materials carried out by most institutions does not go beyond simple agronomic and laboratory assessments. Advanced agronomic evaluations related to determination of nutrient requirements and selection of compatible species for grass-legume mixtures are generally lacking. Apart from a few exceptions, animal experimental evaluation of target species in the sense of grazing trials and feeding trials with penned-in herbivores is also missing. The limitation
has been understandably attributed to a lack of resources (finance, facilities, and expertise). Due to prevailing ignorance of the potential of native genetic forage resources and lack of conservation measures, many potential species are threatened with extinction year after year due to human practices: encroachment of cultivated crops, road construction, urbanization, unjustified land use that devastates the habitats of rare species. Already in the 1980s, warning reports about the eminent danger of extinction of the rarest and most potential native species were made available to the public (Solomon Mengistu, 1988; 2010b; Solomon M. and Alemayehu M, 2015). According to recent observations, incredibly large tracts of natural forest and forest margins, home to various endemic and near-endemic species, have been destroyed for arable farming and urbanization. One can imagine the magnitude of habitat destruction by comparing the present and near past (two decades ago) vegetation status of the Bale Mountains. In less than two decades, many rare and highly potential forage species have been lost due to clearing of the natural vegetation. In the face of these ongoing threats, it is outrageous to learn that a national ex-situ conservation practice does not yet exist.
